vignette: Amara sits across from me, her posture rigid, hands folded tightly over her knees. She tells me about the night everything changed, her voice steady but flat, like a river moving under ice. Two years ago, during the border clashes, she is pulled from her car while traveling home to visit her mother. For eleven days, she is held in a concrete room. The interrogations are methodical, designed to strip away control. She remembers the cold floor, the rhythmic tapping of boots, the way her body learns to go quiet to survive. When the convoy finally breaks through, she does not walk out freely. She is pulled, half-conscious, into the daylight. She returns to the tracks. That is what she does next. She cannot stay home. The silence of her apartment feels heavier than the noise of the engine. On her first return shift, she stands at the front of the locomotive, running her thumb over the emergency brake handle like a rosary bead. The conductor’s seat is supposed to be her place of command. Now, it feels like a cockpit with no escape hatch. Her days are measured in timetables and checks. She boards each car, walking the length with deliberate, measured steps. She counts the doors. She maps the fire exits in her mind. When the whistle blows, her pulse spikes before her brain catches up. She tells me she used to love the rhythm of the rails, the way the wheels clicked over the joints like a lullaby. Now, the sound frays her nerves. At night, the train’s suspension settles through the floor of their third-floor walk-up, and she jolts awake, heart hammering against her ribs, convinced the ground is shaking. Her husband, David, wakes with her. She does not tell him about the dreams where the walls breathe, where the tapping returns. She just rolls to her side and presses her back against his chest, listening for his steady breath, counting his exhales to prove she is alive, that she is here, that it is not happening. Her body still works, but it feels like a borrowed suit. She used to be the one who makes decisions, who keeps the line moving through storms and mechanical failures. Now, she hesitates. She second-guesses radio checks. She wonders if she is reliable, if the passengers sense the fracture in her. When she looks at them through the windshield, she does not see commuters. She sees a crowd that could turn, that could surround, that could pull her off the platform. She has stopped going to the company cafeteria. The clatter of trays, the sudden laughter, the smell of burnt coffee—it all collides. She packs a single sandwich and eats it in the crew bathroom, leaning her forehead against the cool tile until her breathing matches the fluorescent light’s hum. David tries to give her space, to make the bedroom a sanctuary. He notices when she flinches at his touch, when a dropped book sends her scrambling back. He does not push. He just leaves the hallway light on. Amara watches him sleep sometimes, tracing the line of his jaw, trying to remember how to trust the quiet. She wears a simple beaded bracelet her mother gave her, a dark wood worn smooth by time, but now it feels like a reminder of roots she can no longer reach. She tells me she feels like a train that has derailed but keeps moving forward, wheels screeching against empty track. She wonders if the brakes will ever hold again. She comes to my office every Tuesday, not because she expects to be fixed, but because saying the words out loud is the only way to keep them from echoing in the dark.
